Chapter Two: Building Discipline—The Daily Practice of Running and Writing.
Have you ever noticed the special quiet of early mornings? There’s this gentle hush, almost like the world’s holding its breath. For someone stepping into the life of a writer, those hours quickly become sacred. It’s peaceful, with hardly any distractions. The mind, even if it’s a bit sleepy, is open to new ideas.
The routine? It’s simple. Wake up, stretch a little, slip on your running shoes, and head out while the city’s still waking up. The streets are nearly empty—maybe you’ll see a dog walker or a delivery truck, but mostly, it feels like you’ve got the whole place to yourself.
Now, I’ll be honest—running isn’t always easy at first. Your muscles complain, your lungs burn, and there’s this voice in your head saying, “Shouldn’t we just turn back?” But here’s the thing: your body learns. That early discomfort fades. One day, you find your rhythm, and it just clicks. Every run becomes its own little win—a reminder that if you stick with it, you’ll get better.
And guess what? Writing works the same way. Sitting at your desk, staring at a blank page, can feel overwhelming. But if you show up every day—even when you’re not feeling inspired—something changes. You make progress, word by word.
Most people don’t realize just how powerful a simple routine can be. It’s easy to think creativity only strikes in flashes, or that discipline is just for athletes or soldiers. But here’s something worth remembering: our habits shape us in ways we don’t always see. By practicing, daily—whether that’s running or writing—growth isn’t just possible, it’s inevitable. Some days feel amazing, others not so much, but what matters is that you keep going.
Of course, there are setbacks. Injuries happen, or you wake up completely drained. Self-doubt creeps in. On cold mornings, it’s tempting to stay in bed. And when your writing feels stuck, frustration can take over. But the discipline you build through running acts like a kind of armor. Knowing that tough moments will pass—and that sticking with it pays off—makes it just a little easier to keep moving.
Over time, the link between running and writing becomes crystal clear. Both ask you to lean into discomfort, to accept that real progress can be slow and sometimes invisible. Patience is everything. Breakthroughs usually show up after long stretches of struggle. But then, out of nowhere, you hit a runner’s high, or you write a sentence that just feels perfect. And in those moments, all the effort is worth it.
This daily practice—of running and writing—ends up becoming a way to mark time, to notice the seasons changing and the days passing. Every run and every page is a step forward. And as those steps add up, week after week, you start to see real change. Your body gets stronger. Your mind gets sharper. And your writing? It grows more confident and true to who you are.
